requirements.statement: A regression tree's prediction for an observation is the leaf value of the region its predictor values fall into, determined by applying the split rule.

places.quote: every observation that falls in region $R_j$ is predicted by the mean response $\hat{y}_{R_j}$ of the training observations in that region.
**Regression tree prediction:** $\hat{y} = \frac{1}{|R_m|}\sum_{i \in R_m} y_i$ for region $R_m$

requirements.statement: For a linear regression with d predictors fitted to n observations, AIC = (1/n)(RSS + 2·d·σ̂²), where σ̂² is the estimated error variance.

resolution.quote: for a model with $d$ predictors fitted to $n$ observations AIC takes the form below … $$\text{AIC} = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + 2d\,\hat\sigma^2\right)$$
resolution.note: Least-squares AIC = (1/n)(RSS + 2dσ̂²) for d predictors, up to constants. ISLR 2nd ed. (CAS-hosted copy, sha256:f708349f…) §6.1.3, p.234 (PDF 242). Checked by a different agent from the writer.

requirements.statement: When computing AIC to compare models, estimate σ̂² once from the full model containing all predictors (the square of its residual standard error) and use that same value for every candidate model.

resolution.quote: Here $\hat\sigma^2$ is an estimate of the error variance obtained once, from the full model containing all the predictors (the square of its residual standard error), and the same value is used for every candidate.
resolution.note: σ̂² estimated once from the full model containing all predictors and used for every candidate. ISLR 2nd ed. (CAS-hosted copy, sha256:f708349f…) §6.1.3 eq. 6.2 text and footnote 4, pp.233-234 (PDF 241-242). Checked by a different agent from the writer.

requirements.statement: The model with the smallest AIC is preferred when selecting among candidate models.

places.quote: Lower AIC indicates a better model (better fit relative to complexity)
Lower [[AIC]] or [[BIC]] indicates a better trade-off between fit and complexity

requirements.statement: The residual standard error is the square root of the estimated error variance, so squaring it gives σ̂².

places.quote: RSS is the numerator of the **residual variance** estimate: $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{RSS}/(n-p-1)$
and the residual standard error is $\sqrt{\text{MS}_{\text{Res}}}$

requirements.statement: Omitting important explanatory variables from a regression model (underspecification) generally biases the coefficient estimates of the remaining variables, unless the omitted variables are uncorrelated with the included ones.

places.quote: In modelling, bias also arises from the *model* rather than the estimator — an omitted predictor, an ignored [[Interaction]], or fitting a straight line to a curved relationship all bias the fitted values regardless of sample size

requirements.statement: Omitting important variables leaves unexplained variation in the residuals, so the error variance estimate s^2 is inflated, which widens prediction intervals.
The total sum of squares depends only on the response values (their deviations from the mean), so it does not change with which explanatory variables are included in the model.

places.quote: **Decomposition**: $\text{SS}_{\text{Tot}} = \text{SS}_{\text{Reg}} + \text{RSS}$, where $\text{SS}_{\text{Tot}} = \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2$ and $\text{SS}_{\text{Reg}} = \sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2$

requirements.statement: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the true relationship in the data, such as when important variables are left out.

places.quote: **Underfitting** = high bias, low variance: training and test error are both high and close together.

requirements.statement: A predictor in a regression model is statistically significant at level alpha if its p-value is less than alpha, in which case the null hypothesis that its coefficient is zero is rejected.

places.quote: It converts any test statistic onto a common $0$–$1$ scale: reject $H_0$ when the p-value falls below the significance level $\alpha$.
A small p-value (e.g., $< 0.05$) indicates the predictor is statistically significant

requirements.statement: The p-value of a coefficient test is the probability, under the null hypothesis that the coefficient is zero, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained.

places.quote: A **p-Value** is the probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained.
$$\text{p-value} = P(\text{test statistic as extreme or more extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ true})$$

requirements.statement: Cost complexity pruning selects the tuning parameter (and corresponding subtree size) by choosing the subtree that minimizes the cross-validation estimate of prediction error such as MSE.

places.quote: The sequence of subtrees as $\alpha$ increases is **nested and finite**, so [[Cross-Validation]] over $\alpha$ picks the size and the tree is refit on the full data at that $\alpha$

ISLR's Algorithm 8.1 grows a large tree $T_0$, uses cost-complexity pruning (the third block) to obtain the best subtree for each $\alpha$, chooses $\alpha$ by $K$-fold cross-validation, and returns the subtree for that $\alpha$.

requirements.statement: The optimal pruned tree size is read from the cross-validation (test) MSE curve at the tree size where it is lowest, rather than from the training MSE, which keeps decreasing as tree size grows.

places.quote: Cross-validation is what turns the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff]] into a decision: training error falls monotonically with complexity, while CV error is U-shaped, and its minimum marks the right model size
Training RSS always prefers the full tree. The size of the pruned tree must come from cross-validation or a validation set

requirements.statement: A random forest builds many decision trees on bootstrap samples and, at each split, considers only a random subset of m of the p predictors, which decorrelates the trees.

places.quote: A **random forest** is [[Bagging|bagged]] [[Decision Tree|trees]] with one extra step: at *each split*, only a random subset of $m$ predictors is eligible. That decorrelates the trees, so averaging removes more variance than bagging can.

requirements.statement: The m candidate predictors in a random forest are sampled without replacement, so that exactly m distinct predictors are considered.

places.quote: A **random forest** is [[Bagging|bagged]] [[Decision Tree|trees]] with one extra step: at *each split*, only a random subset of $m$ predictors is eligible.

requirements.statement: In a random forest, a fresh random sample of m predictors is drawn at every split of every tree, not once per tree.

places.quote: at *each split*, only a random subset of $m$ predictors is eligible.

requirements.statement: The Tweedie distribution has variance equal to the dispersion parameter times the mean raised to the power p, Var(Y) = phi * mu^p.

places.quote: $$\text{Var}(Y) = \phi\,\mu^{p}, \qquad 1 < p < 2$$
$$E[Y] = b'(\theta) = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(Y) = a(\phi)\,b''(\theta) = \phi\,V(\mu)$$
[[Tweedie Distribution|Tweedie]] with $1 < p < 2$: $\mu^p$

requirements.statement: For 1 < p < 2, a Tweedie random variable is a compound Poisson sum of gamma random variables, so it has a point mass at zero equal to e^(-lambda), the probability of zero claims, plus a continuous positive part.

places.quote: For $1 < p < 2$ it is a compound Poisson–Gamma distribution: a Poisson number of Gamma-sized claims. That gives it a point mass at zero plus a right-skewed continuous part
- $P(Y = 0) = e^{-\lambda} > 0$: the Tweedie is the one member that puts genuine probability on exactly zero while remaining continuous elsewhere

requirements.statement: The Tweedie distribution belongs to the exponential dispersion family (linear exponential family) of distributions used in generalized linear models.

places.quote: The **Exponential Family** is the class of distributions whose density can be written in a common exponential form. It is the set of response distributions a [[Generalized Linear Model]] can use: Normal, Poisson, binomial, [[Gamma]], inverse Gaussian, and the [[Tweedie Distribution]] all belong to it.

requirements.statement: The Poisson distribution is only a limiting case of the Tweedie distribution with 1 < p < 2 as p approaches 1, not a special case within that range of p.

places.quote: | $1$ | Poisson | Counts |

requirements.statement: PCA constructs principal components as linear combinations of the predictors, so it captures only linear relationships among the variables.

places.quote: $\mathbf{z}_m = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\phi}_m$ is the $m$-th **score vector** (principal component)
Every $Z_m$ is a linear combination of all $p$ original predictors
$$z_{im} = \phi_{1m}x_{i1} + \phi_{2m}x_{i2} + \cdots + \phi_{pm}x_{ip}$$

requirements.statement: Principal components are ordered so that the first component captures the largest share of variance in the data, and each later component captures the most remaining variance while being uncorrelated with earlier ones.

places.quote: PCs are **orthogonal** — each successive PC captures the maximum remaining variance
Each later component has the largest variance subject to being uncorrelated with the ones before it, which means perpendicular to them.

requirements.statement: Later principal components, which explain little variance, are the ones that tend to reflect noise, while the first components capture the main structure.

places.quote: The name is geological: the steep face is the components that matter, the rubble at the base is noise

requirements.statement: A loading is the coefficient of a variable in a principal component; a loading near zero means that variable contributes little to that component.

places.quote: $\phi_{1m}, \dots, \phi_{pm}$ are the **loadings** of the $m$th component
A **loading vector** $\boldsymbol{\phi}_m$ holds the weights that define the $m$-th principal component in [[Principal Components Analysis]].

requirements.statement: Principal components are derived features, not predictors, and a variable's small loading on one component does not mean the variable is unimportant or can be discarded.

places.quote: Every $Z_m$ is a linear combination of all $p$ original predictors, so the fitted model still uses every one of them (see [[Variable Selection]]).
As in PCR, the new features are linear combinations of the original predictors, not a subset of them (see [[Variable Selection]]).

requirements.statement: The validation set approach randomly splits the data into a training set and a validation set, fits the model on the training set, and estimates test error from the validation set; different random splits give different estimates.

places.quote: **Validation set:** fit on one part and score on the rest. Simple, but the estimate is variable and overstates the error, because the fit used fewer observations.
ISLR's validation set approach (James et al., §5.1.1) splits the data in two, fits on one part and scores on the other.

requirements.statement: Leave-one-out cross-validation fits the model n times, each time holding out one observation, and averages the n resulting errors; it involves no randomness, so it yields the same estimate on every run with the same data.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.
**Leave-one-out (LOOCV):** $\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \text{MSE}_i$.

requirements.statement: Training on fewer observations tends to give a worse-fitting model, so the validation set approach, which fits on only part of the data, tends to overestimate the test error of the model fit to all the data.

places.quote: **Validation set:** fit on one part and score on the rest. Simple, but the estimate is variable and overstates the error, because the fit used fewer observations.

requirements.statement: LOOCV has low bias because each fit uses nearly all the data, but its fitted models are trained on almost identical data and their errors are highly correlated, so its estimate has higher variance than that of k-fold cross-validation.

places.quote: **Leave-one-out** ($k = n$) is nearly unbiased but has high variance and is expensive
It is slightly more biased than LOOCV but less variable, since LOOCV's $n$ fits are nearly identical and their errors highly correlated.

requirements.statement: k-fold cross-validation with a moderate k (such as 5 or 10) has somewhat more bias than LOOCV but lower variance, since its training sets overlap less.

places.quote: $k = 5$ or $10$ is the standard choice, a bias–variance compromise: each fit uses $(k-1)n/k$ observations, so the bias is modest, and the $k$ training sets overlap less than LOOCV's, so the estimate has lower variance — at a cost of only $k$ fits
It is slightly more biased than LOOCV but less variable, since LOOCV's $n$ fits are nearly identical and their errors highly correlated.

requirements.statement: Training MSE decreases (or does not increase) as model flexibility increases, so it cannot be used to compare models of different flexibility or select the model.

places.quote: The **training error**, measured on the fitting data, is different: it falls automatically as the model becomes more flexible, so it cannot choose between models.
Training MSE falls every time flexibility is added, because a model with as many free parameters as observations can reproduce them exactly.

requirements.statement: Test MSE is the mean squared error of a fitted model on held-out observations not used in fitting, and measures predictive performance on new data.

places.quote: **Test error** is the average error a fitted model makes on observations that were not used to fit it.
the test MSE averages the same squared error over observations that were not used in the fit.

requirements.statement: As flexibility increases, test MSE typically follows a U-shape: it falls to a minimum and then rises, so the best model is the one with the lowest test MSE.

places.quote: By the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff|bias-variance tradeoff]], test error is U-shaped in flexibility: bias falls, variance rises.
The total is U-shaped, and the minimum is the right complexity
Training error keeps falling as a model gets more flexible, while error on new data falls and then rises, a U-shape.

requirements.statement: Overfitting occurs when a model fits noise specific to the training data, shown by training MSE continuing to fall while test MSE rises.

places.quote: **Overfitting** is fitting a model so closely to its training data that it follows the noise in that sample as well as the signal, so that it predicts new observations worse than a simpler model would.
A model with small training error and large test error is [[Overfitting|overfitting]]: it has learned patterns in the training data that arose by chance (*ISLR*, §2.2).

requirements.statement: Test MSE is normally higher than training MSE for any model, so a test MSE above training MSE alone does not indicate overfitting; a small gap between them is not the selection criterion, since an underfit model can have a small gap.

places.quote: Training error below test error does not by itself mean the model overfits. Almost every model has this gap; overfitting means a less flexible model would have predicted better.

requirements.statement: Underfitting occurs when a model is too inflexible to capture the true structure, giving high error on both training and test sets.

places.quote: **Underfitting** = high bias, low variance: training and test error are both high and close together.
Selecting too few variables causes underfitting (high bias)

requirements.statement: Validation set approach: randomly split the data into a training set and a test (validation) set, fit candidate models on the training set, and choose the model with the lowest error on the validation set.

places.quote: ISLR's validation set approach (James et al., §5.1.1) splits the data in two, fits on one part and scores on the other.
**Validation set:** fit on one part and score on the rest. Simple, but the estimate is variable and overstates the error, because the fit used fewer observations.

requirements.statement: K-nearest neighbors regression predicts the response at a point x0 as the average of the responses of the K training observations nearest to x0: f̂(x0) = (1/K) Σ_{xi in N0} yi.

places.quote: **Regression:** $\hat{f}(x_0) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_K(x_0)} y_i$

requirements.statement: With a single predictor, the Euclidean distance between a training point xi and a new point x0 is the absolute difference |xi - x0|.

places.quote: $$d_{\text{Euc}}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} (u_j - v_j)^2}$$

requirements.statement: To find the neighborhood in KNN, compute the distance from the new point to every training observation, rank them, and select the K smallest distances.

places.quote: $\mathcal{N}_K(x_0)$ is the **neighborhood** of the $K$ nearest training points to $x_0$
Gather the fraction $s = k/n$ of training points whose $x_i$ are closest to $x_0$.

requirements.statement: KNN regression is non-parametric: it assumes no functional form for f, so its prediction is a local average and does not use a fitted global model such as the least squares line.

places.quote: KNN estimates **no parameters**: it keeps the training data and does its work at prediction time, finding each new point's nearest neighbors, which can be slow in a large training set

requirements.statement: The lag k sample autocorrelation is r_k = sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_{t-k} - ybar)(y_t - ybar) divided by sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - ybar)^2, using the single overall sample mean and the full-series sum of squares in the denominator.

places.quote: \hat{\rho}_k = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n-k}(y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t+k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t - \bar{y})^{2}}
c_k = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n-k}(x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t+k} - \bar{x})

requirements.statement: The lag k autocorrelation measures the correlation between observations of a time series that are k periods apart.

places.quote: The **autocorrelation function (ACF)** gives the correlation between a [[Time Series]] and itself $k$ periods earlier.
The **autocorrelation function (ACF)** $\rho(h) = \text{Cor}(Y_t, Y_{t+h})$ and **partial ACF (PACF)** describe temporal dependence

requirements.statement: In the lag k sample autocorrelation, the numerator sums only the T-k available pairs of observations while the denominator sums over all T observations, and both use the overall mean rather than separate means for each lagged list.

places.quote: \hat{\rho}_k = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n-k}(y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t+k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t - \bar{y})^{2}}
c_k = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n-k}(x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t+k} - \bar{x})
As in the sample ACF, the sum has $n - h$ terms but is divided by $n$.

requirements.statement: If the sample autocorrelations of a fitted model's residuals all lie within the approximate ±2/√n bands, the residuals show no remaining serial correlation, so the mean model (e.g., the AR order) is adequate.
requirements.concept: Residual Diagnostics for Time Series Models

places.quote: On residuals it is the [[White Noise]] check: all spikes inside the bands means the model has extracted the structure
after fitting, the residual [[Autocorrelation Function|ACF]] should show no spike outside the $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{n}$ bands. A surviving spike means structure the model has missed

requirements.statement: Uncorrelated errors are not necessarily independent; autocorrelation in the squared residuals indicates dependence in the errors' variance (heteroskedasticity) even when the residuals themselves are uncorrelated.

places.quote: The shocks $\varepsilon_t$ are uncorrelated, so their [[Autocorrelation Function|autocorrelation function]] looks like that of [[White Noise|white noise]], but their squares are positively autocorrelated, because a large $\varepsilon_{t-1}^2$ raises $\sigma_t^2$.
uncorrelated does not imply independent without it

requirements.statement: An ARCH(p) model specifies the conditional variance of the error as a linear function of the p previous squared errors: σ_t² = ω + γ_1 ε_{t-1}² + ... + γ_p ε_{t-p}².

places.quote: $$\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \gamma_1\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \cdots + \gamma_p\varepsilon_{t-p}^2$$

requirements.statement: Bursts of large residuals of either sign separated by quiet stretches (volatility clustering), together with positively autocorrelated squared residuals, are the pattern an ARCH model is designed to capture.

places.quote: It describes **volatility clustering**, the tendency of financial returns to have large moves, of either sign, followed by more large moves and quiet periods followed by quiet periods.

requirements.statement: An ARCH(p) process with the sum of the γ coefficients less than 1 is stationary with constant unconditional variance ω/(1 − Σγ_j), so changing conditional variance does not imply non-stationarity or a trend in variability.

places.quote: An ARCH process is heteroskedastic only conditionally. Its unconditional variance is constant when it is stationary, so "ARCH implies non-stationarity" is false.

requirements.statement: Sample autocorrelations of a stationary series die out quickly, whereas slowly decaying autocorrelations suggest non-stationarity that calls for differencing.

places.quote: Slow, near-linear decay signals non-stationarity and calls for [[Differencing]]
an [[Autocorrelation Function]] that decays very slowly and nearly linearly
After one difference the autocorrelations die out quickly — that is stationary, with a small MA(1) or AR(1) left to model.
